text.hook:
"unordered_map lookup is O(1)."
Only on average. Worst case is O(n), and every rehash invalidates your iterators.

Swipe ➜ for the mental model and 6 myths that fail interviews.
text.body:
Inside:
1. Buckets of linked nodes
2. Average, worst and amortized cost
3. When a rehash happens
4. What survives a rehash
5. Custom keys and hash quality
6. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: Buckets, load factor, rehash rules, hash quality, and when to pick something else.

slides.title: A hash table with separate chaining

cards.label: Bucket array
cards.text: Contiguous array of pointers. `bucket = hash(key) mod bucket_count()`.

cards.label: Nodes
cards.text: Every element lives in its **own heap node**. Nodes never move.

cards.label: Lookup
cards.text: Hash the key, jump to the bucket, walk the chain comparing with `==`.

slides.takeaway: Keep apart: the **hash** spreads keys, **equality** decides identity, the **load factor** decides growth.

slides.title: O(1) is an average, not a promise
slides.takeaway: Bad hash, adversarial keys (hash flooding) or a shared stride turn chains into lists.

slides.title: When does the table rehash?
steps: `load_factor() = size() / bucket_count()`, the average chain length
**Before** an insert that would exceed it: rehash first, then insert
Erase and `clear()` never shrink the buckets: use `rehash(0)`

slides.title: Rehash relinks nodes, it does not move them
slides.takeaway: `reserve(n)` = room for n **elements**. `rehash(n)` = at least n **buckets**.

slides.title: The hash and equality contract

cards.label: Contract
cards.text: `a == b` must imply `hash(a) == hash(b)`. Else `find` misses.

cards.label: Missing hash
cards.text: No `std::hash` for `pair`, `tuple`, your struct. Write one.

cards.label: Combine well
cards.text: `h1 ^ (h2 << 1)` is weak: longest chain 50 vs 7 with a mixer (one libstdc++ run, 10000 grid points).

slides.takeaway: Hash exactly the fields `operator==` compares. Never mutate a stored key: `extract`, edit, reinsert.

slides.title: Not always the fastest map
slides.takeaway: Flat maps store elements in one array: often faster, but no reference stability.

items.truth: Average O(1), worst O(n). Insertion is also amortized because of rehash.
Iterators yes. References and pointers stay valid: nodes do not move.
It reserves room for n **elements**. `rehash(n)` is the bucket request.
Not for small sizes, costly string hashes or ordered access: `map` or a sorted vector can win.
The bucket count never shrinks by itself. Use `rehash(0)` or swap.
It does not. Write a hash with a real combiner.

slides.hero:
Average O(1).
Iterators die on rehash.
References survive.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.body: The lookup text arrives at runtime, e.g. read from a socket.

slides.title: Same text. What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: The key type is a pointer: the characters are never looked at
bullets: `buf` holds the same text at a different address: the lookup misses.
`key` is the very pointer that was stored, so it is found.
Two equal literals may or may not share an address (unspecified). Never rely on it.

slides.title: Key by content, not by address
slides.tip: Avoid the temporary `std::string` per lookup with a transparent hash + `std::equal_to<>` (C++20).
slides.takeaway: Pointer keys mean identity, not content.

text.hook:
Point has a defaulted operator==.
So it can be an unordered_map key. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Three lines of code, one familiar struct. Read the first error carefully.

slides.title: Does this compile?

bullets: `std::hash<Point>` is not specialized, so it is **disabled**: not constructible, not callable.
The map's default constructor must build a `std::hash<Point>`, so it is deleted.
`operator==` is already there. Only the hash is missing.

slides.title: Specialize `std::hash` for Point
slides.tip: Or pass a hasher: `std::unordered_map<Point, V, PointHash>`.
slides.takeaway: Unordered keys need a hash **and** equality, consistent with each other.

text.hook:
reserve(1000) forces a rehash.
A reference, a pointer and an iterator all point at the same element.
Which ones are still safe?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: All three lines print "one" on GCC. That proves less than it seems.

slides.title: Which lines are well-defined?

slides.verdict: A. Lines A and B only
slides.verdict_sub: Line C is UB. GCC 11 / libstdc++ still prints `one`, ASan is silent
bullets: `reserve(1000)` changes the bucket count (13 to 1031 on libstdc++): a rehash.
Rehash allocates a new bucket array and **relinks** nodes. Nodes stay put, so `ref` and `ptr` are valid.
Every iterator, `end()` included, is invalidated by the standard.
It works on libstdc++ (iterators are node pointers; even `-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG` is silent). The standard still makes it UB.
slides.wrong: "B: it printed one, so all three are fine"

slides.title: Cache values, not iterators
slides.code:
auto it = m.find(1);
std::string* val = &it->second; // keep

m.reserve(1000);                // rehash

std::cout << *val << '\n';       // fine
it = m.find(1);                 // redo
slides.tip: Know the final size? Call `reserve(n)` once, before inserting and before taking iterators.
slides.takeaway: Rehash invalidates iterators, never references or pointers.

text.hook:
Five int keys: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40.
Print the map, call rehash, print it again.
The keys did not change. Does the output?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Measured on GCC 11 / libstdc++, x86-64. Another library may differ, which is the point.

slides.title: What does this print?

slides.verdict_sub: Observed on GCC 11 / libstdc++, x86-64. The standard leaves the order unspecified
bullets: libstdc++ keeps all nodes on one list. A key landing in an empty bucket goes to the **front**: newest first.
`rehash(1000)` relinks the nodes bucket by bucket. With the identity `std::hash<int>`, the order happens to be ascending.
Another library or version may print something else.
Any rehash can reorder the elements.
slides.wrong: "A: small int keys come out sorted"

slides.title: Need an order? Make one
slides.tip: Two maps with equal contents can iterate differently, yet `==` says they are equal.
slides.takeaway: Never test, log or serialize unordered iteration order.
